prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

No classes here! Why, that is idle talk. The village beau sneers at the country boor; The importuning mendicants who walk Our cites’ streets despise the parish poor. The daily toiler at some noisy loom Holds back her garments from the kitchen aid. Meanwhile the latter leans upon her broom, Unconscious of the bow the laundress made. The grocer’s daughter eyes the farmer’s lass With haughty glances; and the lawyer’s wife Would pay no visits to the trading class, If policy were not her creed in life. The merchant’s son nods coldly at the clerk; The proud possessor of a pedigree Ignores the youth whose father rose by work; The title-seeking maiden scorns all three. The aristocracy of blood looks down Upon the “nouveau riche”; and in disdain, The lovers of the intellectual frown On both, and worship at the shrine of brain. “No classes here,” the clergyman has said; “We are one family.” Yet see his rage And horror when his favorite son would wed Some pure and pretty player on the stage. It is the vain but natural way Of vaunting our weak selves, our pride, our worth! Not till the long delayed millennial day Shall we behold “no classes” on God’s earth.

---

### Option 1: Eloquent Prose (Recommended for essays, speeches, or articles)

> To claim that we live in a classless society is mere illusion. The fashionable village youth scorns the rustic laborer, just as the city mendicant looks down upon the parish poor. In daily life, the factory worker draws her garments back from the kitchen maid, who, leaning upon her broom, remains completely oblivious to the laundress's respectful bow.
>
> Social divides persist at every turn. The grocer’s daughter casts haughty glances at the farmer’s lass, and the lawyer’s wife would never deign to visit the trading class were it not for political expediency. The merchant’s son greets the clerk with a cold nod; the proud heir of an ancient pedigree ignores the youth whose father built his fortune through honest toil; and the title-seeking maiden holds all three in contempt.
>
> The aristocracy of noble birth looks down upon the *nouveau riche*, while the intellectual elite hold both in disdain, worshipping solely at the altar of intellect. Even the clergyman, who preaches that "we are all one family," betrays his hypocrisy through outrage when his favored son seeks to marry a virtuous and lovely stage actress.
>
> This subtle snobbery is merely humanity's vain, natural instinct to elevate its own self-worth. Not until the long-delayed millennial era dawns shall we truly witness a classless society upon God’s earth.

---

### Option 2: Refined Literary / Verse (Preserving the poetic structure)

> To speak of a classless society is pure delusion.  
> The village dandy sneers at the rustic laborer;  
> The city’s persistent mendicant despises the parish poor.  
> The factory worker draws back her skirts from the kitchen maid,  
> Who, leaning on her broom, ignores the laundress’s quiet bow.  
>

> The merchant’s son offers a frigid nod to the clerk;

>
> Such is our vain, inherent instinct to elevate ourselves.  
> Not until the long-awaited millennial day

The claim that social hierarchies do not exist in our society is utter nonsense. In reality, a fashionable town gentleman ridicules an unrefined farmhand, while persistent street panhandlers in the city look down on the local impoverished population. A female factory worker shifts her clothing away to avoid touching a kitchen housemaid; yet, that same housemaid, engrossed in sweeping, ignores a respectful greeting from a washerwoman. 

A merchant's daughter glares haughtily at a rural farm girl, and an attorney’s wife would never socialize with the business class if her own self-interest did not compel her to do so. A wealthy merchant’s son gives a cold, distant greeting to an office clerk, while a person boasting ancient aristocratic lineage completely disregards a young man whose father gained wealth through hard labor. Meanwhile, a woman determined to marry into nobility rejects all of them.

The high-born elite despise the newly wealthy, while intellectuals hold both groups in contempt, placing supreme value on mental brilliance. Even a minister who preaches that all people belong to one equal human family reacts with furious disgust when his favorite son wishes to marry a virtuous and attractive theater actress. 

Establishing these divisions is simply a foolish, human attempt to boost our own fragile self-esteem and sense of importance. True social equality will not exist in this world until a distant, idealized future finally arrives.
outputs.L3:
**The Persistence of Hierarchy: Debunking the Myth of the Classless Society**

Despite modern rhetoric celebrating egalitarianism and meritocracy, the claim that contemporary society has eradicated social classes is a convenient fallacy. In reality, rigid divisions and deeply ingrained prejudices permeate nearly every level of human interaction. Far from living in a seamless, unified world, human beings remain bound by a complex web of social stratification that dictates status, influence, and mutual perception.

Crucially, this class consciousness is not merely an elite obsession imposed from above; it is a impulse that fractures society at every tier. Even within lower-income and working-class communities—where shared economic struggles might logically foster solidarity—individuals continually invent subtle metrics to establish superiority over one another. Minor differences in employment status, neighborhood, or lifestyle choices are frequently weaponized to justify looking down on peers, proving that snobbery is a universal habit rather than an aristocratic privilege.

Across the broader social landscape, these hierarchies are constantly reinforced through a variety of shifting capital markers. Wealth alone does not dictate standing; rather, society maintains intricate distinctions between ancient lineage and newly acquired riches, often disparaging the latter while venerating the former. Furthermore, professional status creates distinct castes, while intellectual elitism grants a refined form of prestige to the educated class, allowing them to look down on others under the guise of enlightenment. Through these intersecting channels of lineage, wealth, career, and intellect, social barriers are continuously erected and maintained.

This pervasive class bias exposes profound moral ironies, particularly within institutions tasked with promoting human equality. Religious leaders, for instance, frequently preach from the pulpit that humanity is a single, undivided family bound by universal brotherhood. Yet, in their private lives and institutional dealings, many of these same leaders display blatant hypocrisy. They readily uphold class prejudices, aligning themselves with wealthy patrons, maintaining social distance from the marginalized, and quietly enforcing the very social divisions their faith explicitly rejects.

Ultimately, social stratification persists because it is not merely an economic system, but a reflection of the human psyche. Rooted in innate vanity, insecurity, and the prideful desire to feel superior to others, the drive to categorize and rank our fellow humans appears almost immutable. Consequently, the vision of a genuinely classless society remains an impossible ideal for the present—a distant, utopian dream that humanity cannot realize until it undergoes a fundamental transformation of its own nature.
outputs.L4:
We live in an era that loudly proclaims its commitment to egalitarianism. Modern democracies celebrate the dismantling of feudal systems, the erosion of explicit caste structures, and the triumph of meritocracy. We assure ourselves that in a world governed by equal rights and digital connectivity, the old boundaries of class have finally dissolved. Yet, this vision of a classless society is largely a comforting myth. Beneath our democratic rhetoric lies a complex, deeply entrenched web of social stratification—one kept alive not by law, but by the pervasive, subtle art of everyday snobbery. 

Far from disappearing, class distinctions have simply evolved into more insidious forms. Economic snobbery, for instance, no longer relies solely on grand displays of aristocratic luxury. Instead, it manifests in the weaponization of taste and lifestyle choices. We observe subtle hierarchies playing out in the most mundane environments: the grocery aisle, where organic, fair-trade, artisanal products act as signals of superior standing; the neighborhood coffee shop, where ordering decisions double as declarations of sophistication; or the subtle condescension directed at those who patronize chain restaurants or shop at discount retailers. Wealth is no longer merely spent; it is curated to signal membership in an elevated social tier.

This stratification extends seamlessly into the realm of work. Occupational snobbery remains one of the most stubborn fixtures of modern life. Despite public platitudes praising "essential workers" or the dignity of labor, society continues to enforce a rigid hierarchy of prestige. The white-collar professional quietly looks down upon the skilled tradesperson, ignoring the financial parity that may exist between them. Within the corporate world itself, endless sub-castes emerge: the tech strategist scoffs at the middle manager, the boutique consultant pities the civil servant, and the creative freelancer views them all as uncultured cogs in a machine. Work is rarely evaluated purely by its utility or earnings, but rather by the cultural capital it confers.

Perhaps the most vicious form of modern division, however, is intellectual and cultural snobbery. Because it masquerades as enlightenment rather than privilege, it often escapes self-scrutiny. It is revealed in how we judge accent, vocabulary, and grammar; in the books on a person’s bedside table; or in the media they consume. To prefer a blockbuster movie over a subtitled indie film, or a popular podcast over an academic journal, is often quietly logged as a moral or intellectual failure. In these subtle interactions, cultural literacy becomes a gatekeeping tool, used to distinguish the "cultivated" from the masses.

Ultimately, these endless divisions reveal a fundamental truth about human nature: class distinctions are not merely the result of flawed economic systems, but an inevitable byproduct of human vanity and pride. As social creatures, humans possess an innate desire for distinction, an insecure impulse to measure self-worth by establishing superiority over others. Whenever an old barrier of class is knocked down, human ego promptly erects a new, more nuanced one to take its place. 

Because snobbery is rooted in the psychological need for status rather than external laws, genuine social equality will remain an unattainable ideal for the foreseeable future. We may successfully legislate equal rights and construct fairer economic frameworks, but as long as human vanity persists, the myth of the classless society will continue to be exposed by the quiet, everyday ways we divide ourselves.
outputs.L5:
Here is a text built around the themes of curiosity, existence, and shared purpose, incorporating your keywords:

***

### The Question That Defines Us

Of all the words in the human language, few carry as much quiet power as **"Why."** It is the first question of a child gazing up at the sky and the final pursuit of the philosopher contemplating the cosmos. "Why" is the engine of discovery; it refuses to accept the world simply as it appears. It demands meaning behind the mundane and purpose behind the chaos. Without "why," history stands still.

It is through this relentless questioning that we begin to understand **"The"** world around us—not just as an abstract concept, but as *the* singular, breathtaking reality we inhabit. We look at *the* vastness of the oceans, *the* intricacy of a single leaf, and *the* quiet resilience of the human spirit. Using the word "the" highlights specificity and significance; it draws our focus to the exact moment we are in and the definitive choices we must make.

Ultimately, these inquiries lead us back to **"Our"** shared existence. Curiosity may begin in the mind of an individual, but its answers belong to everyone. It is *our* story we are writing, *our* planet we are striving to protect, and *our* collective future we are building day by day. When we combine our individual searches for truth, we realize that we are not isolated observers in the universe, but co-authors of a shared destiny. 

To ask *why* is to honor *the* past, navigate *the* present, and take responsibility for *our* tomorrow.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming poem arguing against the belief that modern society is classless, using everyday examples of social snobbery from the working class to the elite.
counterfactuals.output:
They claim the ancient walls are down, the old divisions dead,
That merit rules the modern world and levels us instead.
"A classless age!" the chorus sings, a polite and pleasant lie—
Yet everywhere you look today, the old distinctions fly.

In gated halls where "old cash" reigns, the subtle codes remain:
They sneer at flashy supercars and loud designer chains.
New money buys the penthouse, but it cannot buy the art
Of sounding like you’re born to play a high and privileged part.

Descend into the suburbs where the middle-tier resides,
And see the quiet judgment that the manicured hedge hides.
The organic canvas tote bag is a badge of moral grace;
They wince at plastic lawns and giant TVs out of place.

They judge your choice of words for lunch, your coffee, or your wine,
And draw a subtle, sharp, and unforgiving line.
To use the wrong vocabulary or drink a commercial brew
Is all it takes for them to look straight down their nose at you.

Yet turn toward the working street and find the reverse strain,
Where snobbery still operates inside a different vein.
The brickie mocks the desk-bound clerk whose hands are soft and white,
And scoffs at "fancy" salad shops or being "too polite."

And if a local kid aspires to rise and change his state,
The whispers start: "He’s acting grand," "He’s mocking his old mate."
They pull him down for trying to reach beyond the neighborhood rules,
And sneer at those who read too much or go to higher schools.

So do not swallow fairy tales that rank and caste are gone;
The lines are merely painted now, instead of carved in stone.
We’ve only swapped the top-hats for a quiet, modern sneer—
The velvet rope is hidden, but make no mistake: it’s here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a Victorian-style poem about social stratification and class hypocrisy? Show how every layer of society—from mendicants and factory workers to intellectuals, businessmen, and clergymen—looks down on someone else despite claiming everyone is equal.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath the gas-lit fog of London town,
Where marble spires pierce a soot-choked sky,
A grand conceit is passed from monarch down,
Asserting all are equal in God’s eye.
Yet mark the rung on which each mortal stands:
They preach of grace, with hatred in their hands.

From carved mahogany, the Vicar preaches
That Christ beholds all souls with equal grace;
With practiced tears, the holy man beseeches
His flock to see the Lord in every face.
Yet stepping forth into the cobblestone,
He shrinks from tradesmen, lest his cloak be blown.

The Merchant Lord, whose iron mills devour
The lives of men to build his grand estate,
Declaims that "Merit" rules the present hour,
And any honest soul may challenge fate.
Yet marks the scholar with a sneering eye,
As pedant, fool, and idle passer-by.

The Scholar, in his leather-bound domain,
Pens lofty tracts on Universal Right,
Declaring every man of heart and brain
Is born to walk in Freedom’s equal light.
Yet views the weaver, grime upon his face,
As brutish, coarse, and of a lesser race.

The Weaver, bent beneath the loom’s command,
Rails at the rich who thrive upon his sweat;
He boasts the virtue of the calloused hand,
Where all true laboring souls as equals met.
Yet turns to spit upon the beggar’s rags,
And curses him who in the gutter lags.

The Beggar, huddled in the freezing mud,
Cries out that God made all men from one clay,
Damns those who walk in silk and noble blood,
And begs a penny for his wretched day.
Yet snarls in triumph at the vagrant blind,
And deems himself superior in mind.

From steeple high down to the ditch's seam,
The self-same lie is sung by every tongue:
That human worth fulfills a godly dream,
Where none are high, and none to darkness flung.
Yet step by step, along the ladder’s rung,
Each sneers at him who lingers just below,
And hides his venom in a holy show.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical poem that begins with someone claiming "No classes here!" and then disproves it through vignettes of various professions and social ranks ignoring or scorning one another.
counterfactuals.output:
“No classes here!” the Chairman cried,
With open arms and boundless pride.
“We’ve cast the feudal chains away!
We’re equal in the modern day!”
He beamed, then stepped into his jet,
And stepped on someone’s silhouette.

The Venture Lord in fleece and vest
Agreed that all were truly blest,
Yet sneered at Old Money’s antique crest;
While Old Money thought him an unwashed pest.
The Crypto Bro looked at the pair and cheered:
“Two dinosaur fools!” he quietly sneered.

The Tenured Scholar, draped in tweed,
Proclaimed that all possessed the seed
Of equal intellect and thought—
Then mocked the Adjunct he had bought.
The Adjunct, starving, turned his head
And mocked the Tradesman’s lack of read.

At Whole Foods, where the pure-at-heart
Fill organic baskets in the cart,
The Heirloom Baker looked with dread
At a peasant buying sliced white bread.
While by the till, the Vegan Queen
Glared at a steak with eyes of spleen.

The Uber Black, with leather seat,
Refused to let the Lyft merge in the street.
The Lyft driver scoffed at the DoorDash lad,
Who thought the Amazon van was sad,
Who swore that the guy on the bicycle-rig
Was the lowest parasite in the gig.

The Plumber looked down on the Drywall guy,
Who eyed the Painter with a heavy sigh;
The Painter scoffed at the Landscaper’s grass,
Who thought the whole neighborhood lacked real class.
Each sat on a rung of a hidden wall,
Sustained by the joy of another one’s fall.

The Barista with the handlebar mustache
Tossed a customer’s dark-roast in the trash:
“Pour-overs only,” he hissed with disdain,
“Go back to Dunkin’ you simple-brained swain!”

“No classes here!” the chorus sings,
From valet boys to tech-firm kings.
We’re egalitarian through and through—
Now get out of my sight, I’m superior to you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem about social class hierarchy and human vanity, specifically including a hypocritical minister who preaches equality but refuses to let his son marry a stage actress.
counterfactuals.output:
Upon the pulpit’s carved veneer,
The Reverend stood to guide the weak.
"Before the Lord," he rang out clear,
"The mighty are as are the meek.

"No king is higher than the knave,
No silver soul outshines the clay.
From cradle to the waiting grave,
We walk the selfsame humble way."

The congregation wept to hear
A gospel preached so sweet and wide,
Where vanity was cast severe,
And earthly rank was put aside.

Yet when his son came home that night,
To ask a blessing on a bride—
A lady of the footlight's light,
Who sang where painted curtains slide—

The preacher’s holy blood grew cold,
His brow collapsed in stern disdain.
"A player's girl? A voice for gold?
You wish to drag our noble name!

"She trades in sham and low degree,
A creature of a cheaper sphere!
No tragic actress marries me,
Nor brings her vulgar drama here!"

"Father," the young man softly spake,
"Did you not teach that all are one?
Shall divine truth and mercy break
When claimed in secret by your son?

"She paints her cheeks to play a part,
An honest actor in the light;
While you disguise a haughty heart
To fool the flock on Sunday night."

The shepherd scowled and turned the key,
To shield his rank from public shame,
Lest high-born elders laugh to see
A common scandal smudge his name.

Oh vanity, that builds a throne
Out of the scriptures of the Lord!
He claims the heavens for his own,
Yet wields a petty, worldly sword.

Both play a role—the stage, the nave—
Yet only one deceives the soul:
The actress leaves it at the grave;
The preacher plays the hypocrite's role.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a traditional rhyming poem about classism in America.
counterfactuals.output:
The gilded land where all are born the same,
Or so the grand and ancient myth is told,
Plays out a quiet and unequal game,
Where some inherit dirt, and others gold.

Above the clouds, the towers of glass arise,
In quiet halls where ivory shadows fall;
The distant wealthy gaze with indifferent eyes
Upon the street that stretches past the wall.

They preach that labor yields a sure reward,
That honest sweat will buy a place of pride;
Yet double shifts can scarce a home afford,
While fortunes bloom upon the favored side.

A zip code draws a dark, unyielding line,
And justice weighs the coin within the hand;
For some, the world is built by grand design,
For most, a struggle on a sinking sand.

Behind high gates where silent fountains flow,
The sheltered rest, immune to daily dread;
They rarely see the quiet suffering below,
Nor count the cost of daily, desperate bread.

Though Liberty still holds her torch on high,
Her shadow falls upon a fractured ground—
Where wealth determines who may reach the sky,
And poverty must suffer without a sound.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
